questions.question: Define acids and bases according to Lowry-Brønsted, define a conjugate acid-base pair and an ampholyte, and identify the two conjugate pairs in the reaction of ammonia with water.
questions.expected_answer: According to Lowry-Brønsted, an acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor. A conjugate acid-base pair is two species that differ by exactly one proton — the acid being the species with the extra proton. An ampholyte (amphiprotic substance) is a substance that can act as either an acid or a base depending on its reaction partner; water, the hydrogen carbonate ion and the hydrogen sulfate ion are examples. In the reaction of ammonia with water, ammonia accepts a proton from water to form the ammonium ion, while water becomes the hydroxide ion. Pair one: ammonium (acid) and ammonia (its conjugate base) — they differ by one proton. Pair two: water (acid, since it donated the proton in this reaction) and hydroxide (its conjugate base). In this reaction water acts as the acid, whereas with hydrochloric acid it acts as the base and forms hydronium — which is exactly what makes it an ampholyte.

questions.question: Distinguish between a strong acid and a concentrated acid, giving an example of a concentrated weak acid and a dilute strong acid. Then calculate the pH of (a) 0,01 mol·dm⁻³ HCl, (b) 0,05 mol·dm⁻³ H₂SO₄, and (c) 0,001 mol·dm⁻³ NaOH (Kw = 1 × 10⁻¹⁴), and explain why 0,01 mol·dm⁻³ ethanoic acid has a pH above 2.
questions.expected_answer: Strength describes the fraction of molecules that ionise: a strong acid (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄) ionises completely, a weak acid (ethanoic, oxalic, carbonic) only partially, in equilibrium with its ions and characterised by a small Ka. Concentration describes the amount of acid dissolved per volume of solution, regardless of ionisation. Household vinegar is a concentrated weak acid; the trace HCl in a pool-testing solution is a dilute strong acid. (a) HCl ionises completely: [H₃O⁺] = 0,01 = 10⁻², so pH = −log(10⁻²) = 2. (b) H₂SO₄ is diprotic and donates two protons per molecule: [H₃O⁺] = 2 × 0,05 = 0,1 = 10⁻¹, so pH = 1 (not 1,3 — forgetting the factor 2 is the standard error). (c) [OH⁻] = 10⁻³, so [H₃O⁺] = Kw ÷ [OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴ ÷ 10⁻³ = 10⁻¹¹ and pH = 11. Ethanoic acid at 0,01 mol·dm⁻³ has pH above 2 because it is weak: only a small fraction of its molecules donate protons, so [H₃O⁺] is well below 0,01 and the pH lies closer to neutral (around 3,4).

questions.question: In a titration, 25 cm³ of a sodium hydroxide solution is exactly neutralised by 20 cm³ of hydrochloric acid of concentration 0,1 mol·dm⁻³. Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide. Then explain, using salt hydrolysis, why phenolphthalein is the correct indicator for titrating ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide, while methyl orange suits ammonia titrated with hydrochloric acid.
questions.expected_answer: Convert volumes to dm³: acid 0,020 dm³, base 0,025 dm³. Moles of HCl = c × V = 0,1 × 0,020 = 0,002 mol. The balanced equation HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O gives a 1:1 mole ratio, so moles of NaOH = 0,002 mol. Concentration of NaOH = n ÷ V = 0,002 ÷ 0,025 = 0,08 mol·dm⁻³. Indicator choice: the indicator must change colour at the pH of the equivalence point, which is set by the salt formed. Ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide forms sodium ethanoate; the ethanoate ion is the conjugate base of a weak acid and accepts protons from water (hydrolysis), leaving excess hydroxide, so the equivalence point is basic — above pH 7 — and phenolphthalein, which changes colour in that basic range, marks it correctly. Ammonia with hydrochloric acid forms ammonium chloride; the ammonium ion is the conjugate acid of a weak base and donates protons to water, so the equivalence point is acidic — below pH 7 — and methyl orange, changing in the acidic range, is appropriate. In each case 'the salt takes after its stronger parent': only the salt of a strong acid and strong base (like NaCl) gives a neutral equivalence point.
